candidates.source_name: Athanasius of Alexandria / Epistulae ad Serapionem 1.6
candidates.source_attribution: Athanasius of Alexandria, Epistulae ad Serapionem de Spiritu Sancto (Letters to Serapion on the Holy Spirit, I-IV), in Select Writings and Letters of Athanasius, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers (NPNF), Series 2, Vol. 4, ed. Archibald Robertson (Oxford / T&T Clark, 1892). PD. Greek text in Migne PG 26 (1857). The Serapion correspondence is Athanasius's principal anti-pneumatomachian work, refuting the Tropici denial of the Holy Spirit's divinity and homoousion with Father + Son.
candidates.draft_body:
Athanasius of Alexandria Epistulae ad Serapionem 1.6 (c. 350 AD)

'The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek' — Athanasius marks Pneuma kyriou ep' eme (the Spirit of the Lord upon me) as the PARADIGMATIC communicatio-idiomatum anchor for pneumatology: the Word, qua-his-assumed-humanity, RECEIVES the Spirit (anointed-as-prophet/Messiah, with-the-Spirit, fulfilled at the Jordan-baptism); the Word, qua-his-divinity, SENDS the Spirit (the Pentecost-outpouring, the John-20:22 in-breathing). The Word is simultaneously Spirit-recipient (qua-flesh) and Spirit-sender (qua-Word). Christ-himself at the Nazareth-synagogue (Lk 4:18) applies this verse to himself: sēmeron peplērōtai hē graphē hautē — 'today this scripture is fulfilled.' The Tewahedo epiclesis-of-the-Spirit in the Anaphora rests on this dual-Spirit-economy: the Word who-receives-and-sends the Spirit is the same Word the priestly-prayer invokes.
